Stage 1 · Warm-up

Always there, or there right now?

Eight things you might see in a street. Which ones are always there?

Stage 3 · Grammar

Present Simple and Present Continuous

What is always true, and what is going on around now.

Read what Harry, a London street cleaner, says.
  • I work in a very lively neighbourhood.
  • Today I’m working from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m.
  • My boss checks my work every now and then.
  • I get in trouble if I’m chatting when he arrives.
Which sentences are about his job in general, and which are about today?
The two tenses side by side
Present Simple — usuallyPresent Continuous — now
PositiveHe works outside.He’s working from 7 to 3 today.
NegativeHe doesn’t work at night.He isn’t working in the park today.
QuestionDoes he work alone? — Yes, he does.Is he working now? — No, he isn’t.
Question wordWhere does he work?What hours are you working today?
Time wordsalways · usually · often · every day · never recyclednow · right now · at the moment · today · this week
Ask yourself one question
  • Is it always true, or a routine? → Present Simple
  • Is it happening around now, or temporary? → Present Continuous
  • I live in Karaganda (permanent) · I’m staying with my aunt this month (temporary)
  • Both can be true at once: He works outside, but today he’s working indoors.
Two things to watch
  • -s on he / she / it in the Present Simple: he works
  • State verbs stay simple: I know everyone, not I’m knowing. Also like, want, need, understand.
  • Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: He never works at night.
  • …but after be: It is never dull.

PRESENT SIMPLE. Routines and things that are always true. Add -s for he/she/it; use do / does for negatives and questions.

PRESENT CONTINUOUS. am / is / are + -ing. Happening now, around now, or temporary.

STATE VERBS. know, like, want, need stay in the simple form.

Not “He work outside”, not “I am knowing”, not “Today I work from 7 to 3” when you mean just today.

Lesson 5 uses these tenses inside relative clauses.

PRESENT SIMPLE — FORM. The bare verb, plus -s for he / she / it: I work, she works. Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -ss, -x, -o add -es (watches, goes), and consonant + -y becomes -ies (carries). Negatives and questions use do / does, and the main verb goes back to its bare form: He doesn’t work at night · Does he work alone?

PRESENT SIMPLE — USE. Facts that stay true, habits and routines, and permanent situations: I live here. She works in a bank. The market opens at six. This is the tense of what your street is normally like.

PRESENT CONTINUOUS — FORM. am / is / are + verb + -ing. Negative: isn’t / aren’t working. Question: swap the order — Are you working? Spelling follows the same rules you met with the past: drop a final -e (make → making) and double the last letter of a short verb (sit → sitting).

PRESENT CONTINUOUS — USE. Three jobs. Something happening at this moment (A street performer is juggling outside); something temporary rather than permanent (I’m staying with my aunt this month); and something changing (More and more people are reading in Hindi these days). All three are about now rather than always.

THE TWO TOGETHER. This is what the lesson is really about. The same speaker often uses both in one breath, because both are true: I work in a pedestrian area, but today I’m working from 7 to 3. The first is the job; the second is this particular day.

STATE VERBS. Some verbs describe a state, not an action, and stay in the simple form even when you mean right now: know, like, love, hate, want, need, understand, believe. Say I know everyone here, not I am knowing.

The four to watch: “He work outside” (missing -s) · “I am knowing” · “Does he working?” · “He is never work late”.

Frequency adverbs from Lesson 2 come back in task 6. In Lesson 5 both tenses appear inside relative clauses.

Full grammar reference — Present Simple and Present Continuous

Form

Continuous positiveI am working · he is working · they are working
Continuous negativeI’m not working · he isn’t working
Continuous questionAre you working? · Is he working?
Short answersYes, I am. / No, he isn’t.
Simple, for contrastShe works here. · She doesn’t work on Fridays.

Spelling and sound

-ing: come → coming · run → running · lie → lying · travel → travelling.

When and why we use it

  • Present Simple: usual, repeated, permanent, generally true.
  • Present Continuous: at this moment, around this period, temporary, or changing.
  • Some verbs describe a state, not an action, and normally have no continuous form: know, like, want, need, believe, belong, understand, mean, prefer.
  • The continuous is also used for a temporary situation that is not happening this second: I’m reading a good book at the moment.

Signal words

Simple: every day, usually, on Mondays, always. Continuous: now, at the moment, today, this week, Look!, Listen!

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I am knowing him well. → I know him well.Know is a state verb.
  • Look! It rains. → Look! It is raining.Happening at this moment.
  • He is work today. → He is working today.be + -ing, both parts.
  • She is going to the gym every Monday. → She goes to the gym every Monday.A repeated habit takes the simple.

Don’t confuse it with

I live in Almaty = permanently. I’m living in Almaty = for now, and it will change.
